notes: BATCH_007 Banking and Financial Awareness part: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) across 32 topics, IDs BANK_BFA_001204 to BANK_BFA_001403. Built from sources opened on 2026-11-06 (current RBI Directions of 2025-26 and their amendments, FAQs, notifications and press releases incl. the October 2026 MPC minutes and Monetary Policy Report, MoSPI, BIS, IBBI, SEBI, NSE, AMFI, IRDAI, DFS, static.pib PDFs, and named news or legal pages where no official HTML page could be opened); facts seen only in search results are marked web:search-confirmed; no block was worked around. Only changeable values and dated events carry current_affairs. Computed answers are re-derived with asserts in tools/batch_007/banking.py. Facts tested in BATCH_000-BATCH_006 are not repeated. ai:independent-check marks only the questions a separate fresh solver answered blind and got right with confidence.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, what is the minimum tenor of a domestic term deposit that a bank may offer?

options.text: Fifteen days
Thirty days
Seven days
Ninety-one days

solution.explanation: The Directions fix the minimum tenor of a domestic term deposit at seven days. (For NRE term deposits the minimum is one year, while NRO term deposits follow the seven-day minimum.)
steps: Domestic term deposit → minimum tenor 7 days
solution.why_others_wrong: Fifteen, thirty and ninety-one days are not the prescribed minimum; 15 days was an older minimum and 91 days is a Treasury Bill tenor.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Seven days

fact_checks.claim: Para 10(1): the minimum tenor of the deposit offered shall be seven days.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, how often must a bank credit interest on savings deposits?

options.text: Only at half-yearly intervals
Once a year, on 31 March
Monthly, on the last working day
At quarterly or shorter intervals

solution.explanation: Interest on savings deposits is calculated on a daily product basis, i.e. on the end-of-day balance, and the Directions require it to be credited at quarterly or shorter intervals.
solution.why_others_wrong: Half-yearly and annual credit are longer than the permitted interval; monthly credit is allowed (it is shorter than quarterly) but is not the rule laid down.
solution.final_answer: Option D: At quarterly or shorter intervals

fact_checks.claim: Para 18: Interest on savings deposit shall be credited by a bank at quarterly or shorter intervals.
Para 9(1): Interest shall be calculated on a daily product basis.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, up to what end-of-day balance must a bank pay a single uniform rate of interest on a savings account, irrespective of the amount within that limit?

options.text: ₹1 lakh
₹5 lakh
₹10 lakh

solution.explanation: The Directions require a uniform interest rate on savings balances up to ₹1 lakh; banks may offer differential rates only on any end-of-day balance exceeding ₹1 lakh.
steps: Up to ₹1 lakh: one uniform rate
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹50,000, ₹5 lakh and ₹10 lakh are not the threshold in the Directions (₹5 lakh is the DICGC insurance cover).
solution.final_answer: Option A: ₹1 lakh

fact_checks.claim: Para 9(1)(a): A uniform interest rate shall be set on balance up to ₹1 lakh, irrespective of the amount in the account within this limit. (b) Differential rates of interest may be provided for any end-of-day savings bank account balance exceeding ₹1 lakh.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Universal Banks – Licensing Guidelines, 2025, what minimum share of its branches must a new universal bank open in unbanked rural centres?

options.text: 10 per cent
25 per cent
33 per cent
50 per cent

solution.explanation: The guidelines require a new universal bank to open at least 25 per cent of its branches in unbanked rural centres, i.e. centres with a population of up to 9,999 as per the latest census.
steps: ≥ 25% in unbanked rural centres (population up to 9,999)
solution.why_others_wrong: 10, 33 and 50 per cent are not the prescribed share.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 25 per cent

fact_checks.claim: Para 29: The bank shall open at least 25 per cent of its branches in unbanked rural centres (population up to 9,999 as per the latest census).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: For a commercial bank, which deposit is a 'bulk deposit' under RBI's Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025?

options.text: A single rupee term deposit of ₹1 crore and above
Any savings or term deposit of ₹2 crore and above
Aggregate deposits of one customer of ₹5 crore and above
A single rupee term deposit of ₹3 crore and above

solution.explanation: The Directions define a bulk deposit as a single rupee term deposit of ₹3 crore and above. Interest rates on deposits, including bulk deposits, must be uniform across all branches and are not negotiable between the depositor and the bank.
steps: Amount ₹3 crore or more → bulk deposit
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1 crore is the limit up to which individuals' term deposits must carry a premature withdrawal facility; savings deposits and aggregate holdings are not part of the definition.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A single rupee term deposit of ₹3 crore and above

fact_checks.claim: Para 6(2): 'Bulk Deposit' means Single Rupee term deposits of ₹3 crore and above.
Para 7(2): The interest rates offered on deposits, including bulk deposits, shall be uniform across all branches.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Ramesh ran a sole proprietorship whose current account had a balance of ₹4 lakh when he died. His legal heirs were paid four months later. Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025, what interest is due on this current account balance?

options.text: No interest, because no interest is payable on current accounts
Interest at the bank's one-year term deposit rate, from the date of the claim
Interest at the savings deposit rate, from the date of death until repayment to the claimants
Interest at the savings deposit rate, only for the period beyond 15 days after the claim

solution.explanation: Normally no interest is paid on current accounts. But the Directions provide that balances in a current account of a deceased individual depositor or a sole proprietorship concern earn interest at the savings deposit rate applicable on the date of payment, from the date of death until repayment to the claimants.
steps: General rule: no interest on current accounts
Savings rate from date of death till payment
solution.why_others_wrong: The general no-interest rule has this exception; the term deposit rate and a 15-day start are not in the provision.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Interest at the savings deposit rate, from the date of death until repayment to the claimants

fact_checks.claim: Para 8: No interest shall be paid on deposits held in current accounts. Provided that balances lying in current account standing in the name of a deceased individual depositor or sole proprietorship concern shall attract interest at the savings deposit rate from the date of death till the date of repayment to the claimants.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Universal Banks – Licensing Guidelines, 2025, promoters of a new bank must initially hold at least 40 per cent of its paid-up voting equity, locked in for five years. To what level must this holding be brought down, and within what period?

options.text: 26 per cent, within 15 years
15 per cent, within 12 years
26 per cent, within 10 years
10 per cent, within 15 years

solution.explanation: The guidelines require promoters to hold at least 40% of the paid-up voting equity, locked in for five years from the commencement of business, and to bring it down to 26% within 15 years. The bank must also list its shares within six years and have minimum paid-up voting equity of ₹1,000 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% in 12 years, 26% in 10 years and 10% in 15 years do not match the guidelines.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 26 per cent, within 15 years

fact_checks.claim: Para 15(1): a minimum of 40 per cent of the paid-up voting equity share capital of the bank ... locked in for five years. Para 15(4): shall be brought down to 26 per cent of the paid-up voting equity share capital of the bank within a period of 15 years.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Meena, an individual, placed two term deposits with a bank. (a) ₹2,00,000 for 3 years at 7.25%, which she withdrew after exactly 2 years; when it was made, the bank's rate for a 2-year deposit was 7.00% and its premature-withdrawal penalty is 1 percentage point. (b) ₹50,000, which she withdrew after 5 days. Assuming simple interest, what total interest will she receive under RBI's Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025?

solution.explanation: On premature withdrawal, interest is paid at the rate applicable to the amount and period for which the deposit actually remained with the bank, not the contracted rate, less the disclosed penalty: 2,00,000 × (7.00% − 1%) × 2 = ₹24,000. The second deposit was withdrawn before the 7-day minimum tenor, so no interest is paid on it.
steps: Deposit (b): withdrawn before 7 days → no interest
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹29,000 uses the contracted 7.25%; ₹28,000 ignores the penalty; ₹24,034 wrongly pays interest on the 5-day deposit.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ₹24,000

fact_checks.claim: Para 11(1): Interest shall be paid at the rate applicable to the amount and period for which the deposit remained with the bank and not at the contracted rate. Para 11(2): No interest shall be paid, where premature withdrawal of deposit takes place before completion of the minimum period specified in paragraph 10(1).
Para 10(1): the minimum tenor of the deposit offered shall be seven days.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A cheque for ₹75,000 is returned unpaid for insufficient funds, and the payee receives this information from the bank on 25 March 2026. The payee's written demand notice reaches the drawer on 2 April 2026. Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which statement is correct?

options.text: The notice had to be given by 9 April 2026; an offence arises if the drawer does not pay by 2 May 2026, and the fine can extend to ₹75,000
The notice had to be given by 24 April 2026; an offence arises if the drawer does not pay by 17 April 2026, and the fine can extend to ₹1,50,000
The notice had to be given by 24 April 2026; an offence arises if the drawer does not pay by 2 May 2026, and the fine can extend to ₹2,25,000
The notice had to be given by 9 April 2026; an offence arises if the drawer does not pay by 17 April 2026, and the fine can extend to ₹1,50,000

solution.explanation: Section 138 applies only if the payee makes a written demand within 30 days of receiving the bank's information about the dishonour (25 March + 30 days = 24 April) and the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice (2 April + 15 days = 17 April). The punishment is imprisonment up to two years, or a fine up to twice the cheque amount (2 × ₹75,000 = ₹1,50,000), or both.
steps: Notice: within 30 days of 25 March → by 24 April
Payment: within 15 days of 2 April → by 17 April
solution.why_others_wrong: A 15-day notice window gives 9 April and a 30-day payment window gives 2 May, both wrong; the fine ceiling is twice, not once or thrice, the cheque amount.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The notice had to be given by 24 April 2026; an offence arises if the drawer does not pay by 17 April 2026, and the fine can extend to ₹1,50,000

fact_checks.claim: Section 138: punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both ... the payee ... makes a demand ... by giving a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank ... and the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment ... within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Committee on Customer Service in Banks, set up by RBI in 2010 to examine services to retail and small customers including pensioners, was chaired by:

options.text: M. S. Verma
P. J. Nayak
S. S. Tarapore
M. Damodaran

solution.explanation: RBI constituted the Committee on Customer Service in Banks in 2010 under Shri M. Damodaran, former Chairman of SEBI, to look into services to retail and small customers, grievance redressal and the Banking Ombudsman Scheme.
steps: 2010 customer service committee → M. Damodaran (former SEBI Chairman)
solution.why_others_wrong: M. S. Verma chaired the 1999 working group on weak public sector banks; P. J. Nayak reviewed bank board governance (2014); the Tarapore Committee's 2004 recommendations concerned board-level customer service committees.
solution.final_answer: Option D: M. Damodaran

fact_checks.claim: Committee on Customer Service in Banks ... Chairman: Shri M. Damodaran, former Chairman, SEBI ... constituted by Board Memorandum dated May 26, 2010.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Working Group on Restructuring Weak Public Sector Banks (1999), chaired by M. S. Verma, identified which three banks as weak?

options.text: Indian Bank, Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank
UCO Bank, Central Bank of India and Bank of Maharashtra
Indian Bank, UCO Bank and United Bank of India
United Bank of India, Syndicate Bank and Andhra Bank

solution.explanation: RBI, in consultation with the Government, set up the working group under M. S. Verma, former SBI Chairman. Its report (October 1999) identified Indian Bank, UCO Bank and United Bank of India as weak banks and proposed a comprehensive restructuring of them.
steps: Indian Bank, UCO Bank, United Bank of India
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong option includes banks that the working group did not classify as weak.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Indian Bank, UCO Bank and United Bank of India

fact_checks.claim: Report of the Working Group on Restructuring Weak Public Sector Banks, chaired by Shri M.S. Verma, former Chairman, State Bank of India ... the three banks identified as weak: Indian Bank, UCO Bank and United Bank of India.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Global Trust Bank, a new-generation private bank, was placed under a moratorium on 24 July 2004. With which bank did RBI draft a scheme to amalgamate it?

options.text: Oriental Bank of Commerce
Punjab National Bank
ICICI Bank
Bank of Baroda

solution.explanation: After Global Trust Bank (GTB) was put under a moratorium on 24 July 2004, RBI prepared a draft scheme of amalgamation of GTB with Oriental Bank of Commerce, keeping in view the interests of GTB's depositors; the scheme took effect in August 2004.
solution.why_others_wrong: PNB, ICICI Bank and Bank of Baroda were not parties to the GTB scheme.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Oriental Bank of Commerce

fact_checks.claim: Global Trust Bank Ltd. was placed under an Order of Moratorium on July 24, 2004 ... the Reserve Bank has prepared a draft scheme of amalgamation of GTB with OBC.
Scheme for Amalgamation of Global Trust Bank Ltd. with Oriental Bank of Commerce

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In 2003, which Kerala-based private sector bank was amalgamated with Punjab National Bank?

options.text: Lord Krishna Bank
Nedungadi Bank
Catholic Syrian Bank
Bank of Cochin

solution.explanation: PNB's heritage record notes that the erstwhile Nedungadi Bank Ltd, a Kerala-based private bank, was amalgamated with Punjab National Bank in 2003.
steps: 2003 → Nedungadi Bank Ltd amalgamated with PNB
solution.why_others_wrong: Lord Krishna Bank, Catholic Syrian Bank and Bank of Cochin were not the bank amalgamated with PNB in 2003.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Nedungadi Bank

fact_checks.claim: In 2003, the erstwhile Nedungadi Bank Ltd (e-NBL), a Kerala based private bank was amalgamated with Punjab National Bank.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Arrange the following customer-service milestones in chronological order: I. RBI appoints the Goiporia Committee on customer service in banks II. RBI constitutes the Committee on Customer Service in Banks under M. Damodaran III. The Government appoints the Talwar Committee on customer service in banks IV. Tarapore Committee recommendations lead to Board-level committees for monitoring customer service

options.text: I, III, IV, II
III, IV, I, II
III, I, IV, II
III, I, II, IV

solution.explanation: The Damodaran Committee report recounts the history: Talwar Committee (1975, appointed by the Government of India), Goiporia Committee (1990, appointed by RBI), Tarapore Committee recommendations (2004) leading to Board-level customer service committees, and the Damodaran Committee itself (2010).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other orders misplace Talwar (the earliest), Tarapore (2004) or Damodaran (2010, the latest).
solution.final_answer: Option C: III, I, IV, II

fact_checks.claim: In 1975, the Government of India had appointed the Talwar Committee on customer service in banks. In 1990, RBI appointed the Goiporia Committee on customer service in banks. In 2004, the Tarapore Committee recommendations led to formation of Board level committees.
Committee on Customer Service in Banks ... constituted by Board Memorandum dated May 26, 2010.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: HDFC Ltd merged into HDFC Bank effective 1 July 2023 at a swap ratio of 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares. An investor held 1,000 HDFC Ltd shares on the record date. How many HDFC Bank shares did she get, and what was HDFC Bank's promoter position after the merger?

options.text: 1,680 shares; HDFC Ltd's successor remains the promoter
595 shares; HDFC Bank has no identified promoter
1,050 shares; the Government becomes the promoter
1,680 shares; HDFC Bank has no identified promoter

solution.explanation: Shareholders of HDFC Ltd received 42 HDFC Bank shares of ₹1 each for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares held on the record date (13 July 2023): 1,000 × 42/25 = 1,680. HDFC Bank says that after the merger it has no identified promoter.
solution.why_others_wrong: 595 inverts the ratio (1,000 × 25/42); 1,050 has no basis; HDFC Ltd ceased to exist, and the Government was never the promoter.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1,680 shares; HDFC Bank has no identified promoter

fact_checks.claim: the merger would be effective from July 1, 2023 ... 42 new equity shares of the face value of Re. 1/- each ... for every 25 equity shares of HDFC Ltd. held ... as on the Record Date i.e., July 13, 2023 ... Post the merger, HDFC Bank has no identified promoter.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: One of the six private banks nationalised in April 1980 (each with demand and time liabilities above ₹200 crore) later became, in 1993, the first nationalised bank ever merged into Punjab National Bank. Which bank was it?

options.text: New Bank of India
Vijaya Bank
Punjab and Sind Bank
Andhra Bank

solution.explanation: The six banks nationalised in April 1980 were Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab and Sind Bank and Vijaya Bank. New Bank of India was merged into PNB with effect from 4 September 1993, which PNB records as its first merger of a nationalised bank.
steps: 1980 list: Andhra, Corporation, New Bank of India, OBC, Punjab and Sind, Vijaya
1993 merger into PNB → New Bank of India
solution.why_others_wrong: Vijaya Bank went to Bank of Baroda (2019), Andhra Bank to Union Bank of India (2020), and Punjab and Sind Bank is still a separate bank.
solution.final_answer: Option A: New Bank of India

fact_checks.claim: nationalisation of six Indian private sector banks having demand and time liabilities exceeding Rs. 200 crores each as on March 14, 1980: Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab and Sind Bank and Vijaya Bank.
The merger of New Bank of India with Punjab National Bank came into effect on 4 September 1993.
The first ever and the only merger of a nationalized bank with PNB was in 1993.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Verma Working Group (1999) used seven parameters, along with two criteria of the Narasimham Committee on Banking Sector Reforms, to judge the health of public sector banks. Which of the following was NOT one of the seven?

options.text: Return on assets
Cost to income ratio
Credit–deposit ratio
Staff cost to income ratio

solution.explanation: The seven parameters were capital adequacy, coverage ratio, return on assets, net interest margin, operating profit to average working funds, cost to income and staff cost to income. The group also proposed a government-owned Asset Reconstruction Fund managed by an independent AMC.
steps: Seven parameters: CAR, coverage, RoA, NIM, operating profit/AWF, cost/income, staff cost/income
Credit–deposit ratio is not among them
solution.why_others_wrong: Return on assets, cost to income and staff cost to income are all among the seven parameters.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Credit–deposit ratio

fact_checks.claim: Seven parameters: capital adequacy ratio, coverage ratio, return on assets, net interest margin, operating profit to average working funds, cost to income and staff cost to income ... along with the two criteria recommended by the Committee on Banking Sector Reforms.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Who became the 23rd Governor of the Reserve Bank of India on 4 September 2013?

options.text: Dr. D. Subbarao
Dr. Raghuram Rajan
Dr. Urjit R. Patel
Dr. Y. V. Reddy

solution.explanation: RBI's list of Governors shows Dr. Raghuram Rajan as the 23rd Governor, from 4 September 2013 to 4 September 2016. He succeeded Dr. D. Subbarao and was followed by Dr. Urjit R. Patel.
solution.why_others_wrong: Subbarao (22nd) and Reddy (21st) served earlier; Patel (24th) took over in September 2016.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Dr. Raghuram Rajan

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Section 4 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the capital of the Reserve Bank is:

options.text: ₹100 crore
₹50 crore
₹500 crore
₹5 crore

solution.explanation: Section 4 of the RBI Act states that the capital of the Bank shall be five crores of rupees. Since nationalisation in 1949 this capital is wholly owned by the Central Government.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹50 crore, ₹100 crore and ₹500 crore are not the statutory capital.
solution.final_answer: Option D: ₹5 crore

fact_checks.claim: Section 4: The capital of the Bank shall be five crores of rupees.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Section 13 of the RBI Act, 1934, meetings of RBI's Central Board must be convened by the Governor at least:

options.text: Six times in each year, and at least once in each quarter
Four times in each year, once in each quarter
Twelve times in each year, once a month
Twice in each year, once in each half-year

solution.explanation: Section 13 requires the Governor to convene Central Board meetings at least six times in each year and at least once in each quarter.
steps: Section 13 → at least 6 meetings a year
At least one in each quarter
solution.why_others_wrong: Four, twelve and two meetings a year are not the statutory minimum.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Six times in each year, and at least once in each quarter

fact_checks.claim: Section 13: Meetings of the Central Board shall be convened by the Governor at least six times in each year and at least once in each quarter.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Section 8(4) of the RBI Act, 1934, for what term do the Governor and a Deputy Governor hold office?

options.text: For a fixed term of three years, with one extension of two years
For a term not exceeding five years fixed by the Central Government, with eligibility for re-appointment
For a term not exceeding four years, like other directors, without re-appointment
Until the age of 65 years, as decided by the Central Board

solution.explanation: Section 8(4) provides that the Governor and a Deputy Governor hold office for such term not exceeding five years as the Central Government may fix when appointing them, and are eligible for re-appointment. (The four-year term applies to nominated directors.)
steps: Term fixed by the Central Government
solution.why_others_wrong: The Act does not fix a three-year term or an age limit; the four-year term is for nominated directors.
solution.final_answer: Option B: For a term not exceeding five years fixed by the Central Government, with eligibility for re-appointment

fact_checks.claim: Section 8(4): The Governor and a Deputy Governor shall hold office for such term not exceeding five years as the Central Government may fix when appointing them, and shall be eligible for re-appointment.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of RBI Governors is correctly shown as predecessor → immediate successor?

options.text: Dr. Bimal Jalan → Dr. C. Rangarajan
Dr. Raghuram Rajan → Dr. D. Subbarao
Dr. Y. V. Reddy → Dr. D. Subbarao
Dr. Urjit R. Patel → Dr. Raghuram Rajan

solution.explanation: RBI's list shows Rangarajan (1992–1997), Jalan (1997–2003), Reddy (6 September 2003 – 5 September 2008), Subbarao (5 September 2008 – 4 September 2013), Rajan (2013–2016) and Patel (2016–2018). So Reddy was succeeded by Subbarao.
steps: Order: Rangarajan → Jalan → Reddy → Subbarao → Rajan → Patel → Das
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are reversed: Rangarajan preceded Jalan, Subbarao preceded Rajan, and Rajan preceded Patel.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Dr. Y. V. Reddy → Dr. D. Subbarao

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: At its 623rd meeting on 22 May 2026, RBI's Central Board approved what amount as surplus transfer to the Central Government for the accounting year 2025-26?

solution.explanation: The Board, chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra in Mumbai, approved a record surplus transfer of ₹2,86,588.46 crore for 2025-26, after transferring ₹1,09,379.64 crore to the Contingent Risk Buffer.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,09,379.64 crore is the amount transferred to the Contingent Risk Buffer, not to the Government; ₹2,48,700 crore and ₹3,95,972.10 crore are not the surplus the Board approved.
solution.final_answer: Option D: ₹2,86,588.46 crore

fact_checks.claim: The Board approved the transfer of surplus of ₹2,86,588.46 crore to the Central Government for the accounting year 2025-26.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Consider the following statements about the decisions of RBI's Central Board on 22 May 2026: I. Under the revised Economic Capital Framework, the Contingent Risk Buffer (CRB) can be held between 4.5% and 7.5% of the size of RBI's balance sheet. II. The Board decided to keep the CRB at the top of this range, 7.5% of the balance sheet. III. The Board transferred ₹1,09,379.64 crore towards the CRB for 2025-26. Which of the above is/are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

solution.explanation: RBI's release says the revised ECF allows the CRB to be maintained between 4.5% and 7.5% of the balance sheet; the Board decided to transfer ₹1,09,379.64 crore to the CRB and to maintain it at 6.5%, not 7.5%. The surplus transferred to the Government was ₹2,86,588.46 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option that includes II is wrong because the CRB was kept at 6.5%.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: the Board decided to transfer ₹1,09,379.64 crore towards the CRB for FY 2025-26 ... maintain the CRB at 6.5 per cent of the Balance Sheet size ... between the range of 4.5 per cent and 7.5 per cent of the size of the Balance Sheet.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Section 23 of the RBI Act, 1934, the issue of bank notes is conducted by RBI in:

options.text: The Department of Currency Management of the Ministry of Finance
An Issue Department, kept wholly separate from the Banking Department
The Banking Department, together with Government business
Its wholly owned subsidiary, Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran

solution.explanation: Section 23 provides that the issue of bank notes shall be conducted by the Bank in an Issue Department, which shall be separated and kept wholly distinct from the Banking Department.
solution.why_others_wrong: The Finance Ministry does not issue notes; the Banking Department handles banking business; BRBNMPL only prints notes.
solution.final_answer: Option B: An Issue Department, kept wholly separate from the Banking Department

fact_checks.claim: Section 23: The issue of bank notes shall be conducted by the Bank in an Issue Department which shall be separated and kept wholly distinct from the Banking Department.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, how can a series of bank notes of any denomination be made to cease to be legal tender?

options.text: By a Central Government notification in the Gazette, on the recommendation of RBI's Central Board
By a resolution of RBI's Central Board alone, without Government involvement
By an Act of Parliament amending the Coinage Act, 2011
By an order of the RBI Governor with the approval of the President

solution.explanation: Section 26(2) empowers the Central Government, on the recommendation of the Central Board, to declare by notification in the Gazette of India that any series of bank notes of any denomination shall cease to be legal tender.
steps: Central Government notifies in the Gazette
solution.why_others_wrong: The Central Board cannot act alone; the Coinage Act deals with coins; there is no Governor-President route.
solution.final_answer: Option A: By a Central Government notification in the Gazette, on the recommendation of RBI's Central Board

solution.final_answer: Option C: Two ICEs, by credit rating agencies specifically authorised by RBI

fact_checks.claim: Plans involving restructuring or change in ownership where the aggregate exposure is ₹100 crore or more 'shall require independent credit evaluation of the residual debt by credit rating agencies' specifically authorised by the Reserve Bank (para 32).
'accounts with aggregate exposure of ₹500 crore and above shall require two such independent credit evaluations' (para 34).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, the 'specified period' after a resolution plan is implemented (relevant for upgrading a restructured account) runs from the date of implementation until at least what share of the outstanding principal under the plan (plus any capitalised interest) is repaid?

options.text: 10 per cent
25 per cent
50 per cent
20 per cent

solution.explanation: The Directions define two periods from the date of implementation of the resolution plan: the 'monitoring period' runs until at least 10% of the outstanding principal (plus sanctioned interest capitalisation) is repaid, and the 'specified period' runs until at least 20% is repaid. An account can be upgraded only if it performs satisfactorily during the specified period.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% defines the monitoring period, not the specified period; 25% and 50% are not used in either definition.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 20 per cent

fact_checks.claim: 'specified period' shall mean the period from the date of implementation of resolution plan up to the date by which at least 20 per cent of the outstanding principal debt as per the resolution plan and interest capitalisation sanctioned as part of the restructuring, if any, is repaid (para 6(16)); the 'monitoring period' uses a 10 per cent threshold (para 6(8)).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Lenders' aggregate exposure to Company X is ₹900 crore. Its restructuring plan gets credit opinions on the residual debt of RP3 from one RBI-authorised credit rating agency and RP5 from another. Under RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, what is the position?

options.text: The plan cannot be implemented, since both required opinions must be RP4 or better
The plan can be implemented, since the better opinion (RP3) is above RP4
The plan can be implemented, since the average of RP3 and RP5 is RP4
The plan can be implemented if 75% of lenders by value approve it despite the RP5 opinion

solution.explanation: An exposure of ₹900 crore (≥ ₹500 crore) needs two independent credit evaluations. Only plans that receive a credit opinion of RP4 (moderate degree of safety) or better for the residual debt from the required number of agencies can be implemented. RP5 signals a moderate risk of default, so one of the two required opinions fails the test.
steps: Each required opinion must be RP4 or better
RP5 is worse than RP4 → plan not eligible
solution.why_others_wrong: The rule is not satisfied by the better opinion or by an 'average' rating; lender approval cannot override the ICE condition.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The plan cannot be implemented, since both required opinions must be RP4 or better

fact_checks.claim: 'Only such resolution plans which receive a credit opinion of RP4 or better for the residual debt' from the required number of credit rating agencies shall be considered for implementation (para 35); RP4 denotes a moderate degree of safety and RP5 a moderate risk of default (para 33).
'accounts with aggregate exposure of ₹500 crore and above shall require two such independent credit evaluations' (para 34).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, the Chapter IV timelines for implementing a resolution plan apply from a reference date that depends on the lenders' aggregate exposure. Consider three borrowers: P (aggregate exposure ₹2,400 crore), Q (₹1,600 crore) and R (₹1,200 crore). Which is correct?

options.text: P, Q and R all from 7 June 2019
P from 7 June 2019 and Q from 1 January 2020; R is not subject to Chapter IV
P from 1 January 2020 and Q from 7 June 2019; R from 1 April 2020
Only P, from 7 June 2019; Q and R are not subject to Chapter IV

solution.concept: Reference dates under the prudential framework
solution.explanation: The table of reference dates sets 7 June 2019 for accounts with aggregate exposure of ₹2,000 crore and above, and 1 January 2020 for ₹1,500 crore and above but below ₹2,000 crore; for accounts below ₹1,500 crore the date is to be announced, and such accounts are not subject to the Chapter IV requirements.
steps: R: below ₹1,500 crore → not subject to Chapter IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The dates are tiered, not uniform; they are not reversed; and Q (above ₹1,500 crore) is covered.
solution.final_answer: Option B: P from 7 June 2019 and Q from 1 January 2020; R is not subject to Chapter IV

fact_checks.claim: Reference dates (para 42): aggregate exposure of ₹2,000 crore and above – June 07, 2019; ₹1,500 crore and above but less than ₹2,000 crore – January 1, 2020; less than ₹1,500 crore – to be announced. Accounts with aggregate exposure below ₹1,500 crore are not subject to the Chapter IV requirements (para 43).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about remedies against measures taken under the SARFAESI Act:
I. Any person aggrieved, including the borrower, may apply to the Debts Recovery Tribunal within 45 days of the date on which the measure was taken.
II. An appeal against the DRT's order lies to the Appellate Tribunal within 30 days of receipt of the order.
III. A borrower's appeal is entertained only on deposit of 75% of the debt due, which the Appellate Tribunal may reduce to not less than 50%.
Which of the above is/are correct?

options.text: II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III
I and II only

solution.explanation: Under Section 17, any person aggrieved by a measure under Section 13(4), including the borrower, can apply to the DRT within 45 days of the date the measure was taken. Under Section 18, an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal within 30 days of receipt of the DRT's order; a borrower must deposit 50% of the debt due, which the Appellate Tribunal may reduce, for reasons recorded, to not less than 25%.
steps: S.17: DRT within 45 days of the measure → I correct
S.18: appeal within 30 days → II correct
Pre-deposit is 50%, reducible to 25% (not 75%/50%) → III wrong
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement III misstates the pre-deposit (75% was the DRT pre-deposit struck down in Mardia Chemicals), so any option containing III is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Section 17(1): 'any person aggrieved, including the borrower' may apply 'to apply to the Tribunal within forty five days of the date on which the measure was taken'.

An appeal may be filed 'within thirty days of receipt of the order', and 'no appeal by a borrower is entertained unless it deposits fifty per cent of the amount of debt due', reducible to 'not less than twenty five per cent'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: After reviewing the Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) framework in May 2026, what did RBI decide?

options.text: To activate the CCyB at 0.5% of risk-weighted assets, based on the credit-to-GDP gap
To activate the CCyB at 1% of risk-weighted assets, based on the gross NPA ratio
Not to activate the CCyB at that time, with the credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator
To replace the CCyB with a higher capital conservation buffer of 3.5%

solution.explanation: The CCyB is a Basel III buffer built up in good times for use in a downturn. In its review of 18 May 2026, RBI said, based on empirical analysis of CCyB indicators, that it was not necessary to activate the CCyB at that point. The framework uses the credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator, with supplementary indicators.
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI did not activate the buffer at any rate, the GNPA ratio is not the main indicator, and the capital conservation buffer was not changed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Not to activate the CCyB at that time, with the credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator

fact_checks.claim: Review of Requirement of Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer: 'it has been decided that it is not necessary to activate CCyB at this point in time'; the framework uses the 'credit-to-GDP gap as the main indicator'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio standard, Level 2 assets can make up at most what share of a bank's stock of high-quality liquid assets (HQLA)?

solution.explanation: HQLA consists of Level 1 assets, which can be included without limit, and Level 2 assets, which cannot exceed 40% of the liquidity reserve. Within Level 2, the riskier Level 2B assets cannot exceed 15% of the HQLA stock.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% is the cap on Level 2B alone; 25% and 60% are not Basel caps (60% was the initial LCR phase-in level).
solution.final_answer: Option B: 40%

fact_checks.claim: 'Level 1 assets, which can be included without limit' and 'Level 2 assets, which cannot exceed 40% of the liquidity reserve'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: From which date did the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) become a Basel minimum standard for internationally active banks?

options.text: 1 January 2018
1 January 2015
1 January 2019
1 January 2023

solution.explanation: The NSFR, which requires available stable funding to at least equal required stable funding (a ratio of at least 100%), became a minimum standard for all internationally active banks on a consolidated basis on 1 January 2018.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2015 was when the LCR began its phase-in at 60%; 2019 was when the LCR reached 100%; 2023 is not the NSFR date.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 1 January 2018

fact_checks.claim: 'The NSFR became a minimum standard applicable to all internationally active banks on a consolidated basis on 1 January 2018'.
LCR phase-in: 'the requirement set at 60% and rising by 10 percentage points annually to reach 100% on 1 January 2019'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's capital adequacy amendment directions of 7 October 2026, what risk weight applies to a commercial bank's trade exposure to a qualifying central counterparty (QCCP) when it acts as a clearing member for its own purposes, in OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and securities financing transactions?

options.text: 0 per cent
2 per cent
20 per cent
100 per cent

solution.explanation: The Twelfth Amendment Directions revised the treatment of clearing member banks to align with international standards: a 2% risk weight applies to the bank's trade exposure to a QCCP for OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and SFTs. The same 2% applies where the bank, offering client clearing, must reimburse clients for losses if the QCCP defaults. Parallel amendments were issued for SFBs, payments banks and AIFIs the same day.
steps: Bank = clearing member of a QCCP (own purposes)
Trade exposure (OTC, ETD, SFT) → 2% risk weight
solution.why_others_wrong: QCCP trade exposures are not risk-free (0%), and 20% and 100% are far above the prescribed weight.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 2 per cent

fact_checks.claim: 'Where a bank acts as a clearing member of a QCCP for its own purposes, a risk weight of 2 per cent shall be applied' to the bank's trade exposure to the QCCP in respect of OTC derivatives transactions, exchange traded derivatives transactions, and SFTs.
SFB amendment of the same date: trade exposure to a QCCP from OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and SFTs carries a 2% risk weight.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio standard, which statement about Level 2A and Level 2B assets is correct?

options.text: Level 2A assets take no haircut; Level 2B assets take a 15% haircut and cannot exceed 40% of HQLA
Level 2A assets take a 50% haircut; Level 2B assets cannot be included in HQLA at all
Both take a 15% haircut, and together they cannot exceed 15% of HQLA
Level 2A assets take a 15% haircut; Level 2B assets take higher haircuts and cannot exceed 15% of HQLA

solution.explanation: Level 2A assets are subject to a 15% haircut. Level 2B assets carry higher haircuts and cannot exceed 15% of the stock of HQLA. All Level 2 assets together cannot exceed 40%.
steps: Level 2B: higher haircuts, cap 15% of HQLA
solution.why_others_wrong: Level 2A does take a haircut; Level 2B can be included (within its cap); the 15% cap is on Level 2B only, while all Level 2 assets are capped at 40%.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Level 2A assets take a 15% haircut; Level 2B assets take higher haircuts and cannot exceed 15% of HQLA

fact_checks.claim: 'Level 2A assets, whose value is subject to a 15% haircut' and 'Level 2B assets, which are subject to higher haircuts but cannot exceed 15% of the stock of HQLA'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's amended leverage ratio framework (directions of 23 October 2026, effective 1 April 2027), a bank's derivative netting set has a replacement cost of ₹20 crore and an aggregate add-on of ₹30 crore, and the bank has received collateral of ₹15 crore from the counterparty. Applying the framework's formula for derivative exposures (with the alpha it prescribes and the PFE multiplier fixed at one), what is the leverage ratio exposure for this netting set?

options.text: ₹70 crore
₹49 crore
₹50 crore
₹62 crore

solution.concept: Derivative exposures in the leverage ratio (SA-CCR)
solution.explanation: For the leverage ratio, derivative exposure = alpha × (RC + PFE), with alpha = 1.4 and the PFE multiplier fixed at one, so PFE equals the aggregate add-on. Collateral received from the counterparty does not reduce the exposure measure. Exposure = 1.4 × (20 + 30) = ₹70 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹49 crore wrongly deducts the collateral; ₹50 crore omits the alpha of 1.4; ₹62 crore applies alpha only to the add-on.
solution.final_answer: Option A: ₹70 crore

fact_checks.claim: 'Exposure measure = alpha * (RC + PFE)', where 'alpha is 1.4'; 'For the purposes of the leverage ratio framework, the multiplier is fixed at one.'
'a bank shall not reduce the leverage ratio exposure measure amount by any collateral received from the counterparty.'

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Commercial Banks – Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk Directions, 2026 (effective 1 April 2027), a bank's capital requirement for market risk computed under the simplified standardised approach is ₹240 crore. What are its risk-weighted assets for market risk?

options.text: ₹2,400 crore
₹2,667 crore
₹3,000 crore
₹1,920 crore

solution.concept: Converting a capital charge into RWAs
solution.explanation: Banks must use the simplified standardised approach (SSA) for market risk, and the risk-weighted assets are obtained by multiplying the capital requirement by 12.5 (the reciprocal of 8%). So RWA = 240 × 12.5 = ₹3,000 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: Multiplying by 10, dividing by 9% (the minimum CRAR) or multiplying by 8 are not the prescribed conversion.
solution.final_answer: Option C: ₹3,000 crore

fact_checks.claim: 'A bank shall use the simplified standardised approach (SSA) for computing risk-weighted assets for market risk', by 'multiplying the capital requirements calculated as set out in paragraph 40 by a factor of 12.5.' These Directions shall come into effect from April 1, 2027.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Basel III LCR standard, a bank holds Level 1 assets of ₹450 crore and Level 2A assets with a market value of ₹480 crore; it has no Level 2B assets. Its total net cash outflows over the next 30 days are ₹700 crore. Applying the Level 2A haircut and the cap on Level 2 assets, what is its LCR?

options.text: About 122.6%; it meets the 100% minimum
About 113.3%; it meets the 100% minimum
About 75.6%; it falls short of the 100% minimum
About 107.1%; it meets the 100% minimum

solution.explanation: Level 2A after the 15% haircut = 480 × 0.85 = ₹408 crore. Level 2 can be at most 40% of HQLA, i.e. at most 40/60 of Level 1 = 300. So eligible Level 2A = ₹300 crore and HQLA = 450 + 300 = ₹750 crore. LCR = 750 ÷ 700 ≈ 107.1%.
solution.shortcut: A 40% cap on Level 2 means Level 2 can be at most two-thirds of Level 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: 122.6% ignores the 40% cap; 113.3% wrongly takes 40% of the uncapped total; 75.6% applies the 15% Level 2B cap to Level 2A assets.
solution.final_answer: Option D: About 107.1%; it meets the 100% minimum

fact_checks.claim: 'Level 2 assets, which cannot exceed 40% of the liquidity reserve'; 'Level 2A assets, whose value is subject to a 15% haircut'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's PSL Directions, 2025, what is the total priority sector lending target for Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks?

options.text: 60% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
40% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
75% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
50% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

solution.explanation: Paragraph 7.2 of the PSL Directions sets UCB targets as a percentage of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher: total priority sector 60%, micro enterprises 7.5% and advances to weaker sections 12%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% is the target for domestic commercial banks, 75% for RRBs, and 50% is not a prescribed PSL target.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 60% of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

fact_checks.claim: 'The priority sector lending targets for UCBs shall be as follows': Total Priority Sector 60%; Micro Enterprises 7.5%; Advances to Weaker Sections 12% (targets as a percentage of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the PSL Directions, 2025, what is the sub-target for advances to weaker sections for Regional Rural Banks?

options.text: 12 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
15 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
10 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher
18 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

solution.concept: Weaker sections sub-target by bank type
solution.explanation: The weaker sections sub-target is 12% for domestic commercial banks (and foreign banks with 20 or more branches) and for SFBs, but RRBs, with their rural focus, have a higher sub-target of 15%. It does not apply to foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12% is for commercial banks and SFBs; 10% is the small and marginal farmers sub-target; 18% is the agriculture target.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 15 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher

fact_checks.claim: Advances to Weaker Sections: Domestic Commercial Banks & Foreign Banks with 20 branches and above – '12 percent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher'; Regional Rural Banks – '15 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE, whichever is higher'; Small Finance Banks – 12 percent.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Can a bank use its export credit portfolio as the underlying for issuing 'PSLC – General', according to RBI's PSL FAQs?

options.text: No, export credit can back only PSLCs issued by foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches
No, PSLC – General can be backed only by agriculture and micro enterprise loans
Yes, provided the export credit is eligible for PSL classification under the criteria for domestic banks
Yes, without any condition, since all export credit is priority sector

solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs say export credit can be used as the underlying for PSLC – General, but the issuing bank must ensure that the export credit portfolio is eligible for priority sector classification under the criteria applicable to domestic banks.
steps: PSLC – General counts towards the overall PSL target
Export credit may back it if PSL-eligible
solution.why_others_wrong: Export credit is not restricted to foreign banks' PSLCs; PSLC – General is not limited to agriculture or micro-enterprise loans; and export credit qualifies only if it meets the PSL criteria.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Yes, provided the export credit is eligible for PSL classification under the criteria for domestic banks

fact_checks.claim: Export credit can be the underlying for PSLC – General, provided the bank ensures that the export credit portfolio 'is eligible for priority sector classification' as per the criteria for domestic banks.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On RBI's e-Kuber portal, a bank places a buy order for PSLCs of ₹100 lakh at a premium of up to 2%. Sale offers were placed in this order of time: ₹50 lakh at 2.0%, ₹25 lakh at 1.5% and ₹50 lakh at 1.8%. Following RBI's matching rule, what total premium will the buyer pay?

options.text: ₹1.775 lakh
₹2.000 lakh
₹1.825 lakh
₹1.767 lakh

solution.explanation: Orders are matched at the lowest sale offer first, and only then by time (FIFO). So ₹25 lakh is bought at 1.5% (₹0.375 lakh), ₹50 lakh at 1.8% (₹0.90 lakh) and the remaining ₹25 lakh at 2.0% (₹0.50 lakh): total ₹1.775 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2.000 lakh assumes the buyer's own 2% bid applies throughout; ₹1.825 lakh matches in order of time instead of price; ₹1.767 lakh uses a simple average of the three rates.
solution.final_answer: Option A: ₹1.775 lakh

fact_checks.claim: Matching follows the lowest sale offer first, then first-in-first-out; in the FAQ's example of a buyer at 2% with sellers at 1.5%, 1.8% and 2%, 'the portal will first match with the sale deal at 1.5%', then moves to 1.8% and 2% for remaining units.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
RBI gives higher or lower weights to incremental priority sector credit depending on the district's per capita PSL. Consider the following statements, according to RBI's PSL FAQs:
I. If a bank's credit in a district declines, the weighted incremental credit for that district is taken as zero.
II. Loans bought through Inter Bank Participation Certificates (IBPCs) from another bank in a low-credit district earn the higher weight.
III. Credit is mapped to a district on the basis of its place of utilisation.
Which of the above is/are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III

solution.explanation: Incremental credit in lower-credit districts gets a 125% weight and in higher-credit districts 90%. Only organic credit (disbursed directly, with borrower details on the bank's books) counts; routes such as securitised assets, direct assignment, IBPCs, PSLCs and on-lending through NBFCs, MFIs or HFCs are excluded. A decline gives a weighted incremental credit of zero, and credit is mapped by place of utilisation.
steps: II: IBPCs excluded from weights → wrong
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is wrong because IBPCs are one of the seven indirect routes excluded from the weighting, so any option containing II is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: 'If there is a decline in credit, the weighted incremental credit will be zero (0).' Credit is mapped to a district based on its place of utilization.
Only organic credit counts for incremental weights; excluded routes include 'Inter Bank Participation Certificates (IBPCs)' and 'Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs)'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank has two education loans to individuals. Loan A was sanctioned for ₹25 lakh, but accrued interest during the repayment moratorium has taken the outstanding to ₹26.4 lakh. Loan B was sanctioned for ₹22 lakh and has ₹21 lakh outstanding. Applying RBI's PSL FAQ on education loans whose outstanding exceeds the limit because of interest accrued during the moratorium, how much of the two outstandings together counts as priority sector?

options.text: ₹46.0 lakh
₹21.0 lakh
₹47.0 lakh
₹47.4 lakh

solution.explanation: Education loans to individuals qualify up to ₹25 lakh. When the sanctioned limit is within ₹25 lakh, the entire outstanding counts as PSL even if accrued moratorium interest pushes it above ₹25 lakh. Both loans are within the limit, so 26.4 + 21 = ₹47.4 lakh counts.
steps: Loan A: limit ₹25 lakh (within cap) → full ₹26.4 lakh counts
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹46.0 lakh wrongly caps Loan A at ₹25 lakh; ₹21.0 lakh wrongly excludes Loan A; ₹47.0 lakh uses Loan B's sanctioned amount instead of its outstanding.
solution.final_answer: Option D: ₹47.4 lakh

fact_checks.claim: Outstanding may exceed ₹25 lakh due to 'accrued interest due to moratorium on repayment during the study period'; if the sanctioned limit is within ₹25 lakh, the full outstanding counts toward PSL.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Two borrowers take bank loans for PSL-eligible activities: a partnership firm in which three of its five partners belong to a specified minority community, and a company in which three of its five directors belong to that community. According to RBI's PSL FAQs, which can be counted as advances to specified minority communities (a weaker sections category)?

options.text: Only the company's loan
Both loans, since the majority test is met in each
Only the partnership firm's loan
Neither loan, since only individuals can be counted

solution.explanation: A partnership firm whose majority partners belong to a specified minority community can be treated as an advance to minority communities. A company is a separate legal entity, so advances to it cannot be classified as advances to specified minority communities, whoever its directors are.
steps: Partnership firm: majority partners from minority → eligible
Company: separate legal entity → not eligible
solution.why_others_wrong: The company does not qualify, so options including it are wrong; firms are not excluded, as RBI expressly allows partnership firms with majority minority partners.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Only the partnership firm's loan

fact_checks.claim: A partnership firm whose majority partners belong to a specified minority community can be treated as a minority-community advance; however, 'A company has a separate legal entity', so its advances 'cannot be classified as advances to the specified minority communities.'

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about trading of Priority Sector Lending Certificates on RBI's e-Kuber portal, according to RBI's PSL FAQs:
I. The premium is settled in real time by debiting/crediting the banks' current accounts with RBI, with no separate RTGS transaction.
II. The portal levies a transaction charge on each lot traded.
III. The tax treatment of PSLC trading is left to banks to determine under the applicable tax laws.
Which of the above is/are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I only

solution.explanation: Premiums on matched PSLC deals are settled in real time through the banks' current accounts with RBI, so no separate RTGS is needed. There are no transaction charges on the e-Kuber PSLC module, and RBI leaves the tax treatment to banks under the applicable tax laws.
steps: I: real-time settlement via RBI current accounts → correct
III: tax treatment left to banks → correct
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false, so options with II are wrong; 'I only' omits the correct statement III.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: Premiums are settled in real time; the participating banks' RBI current accounts are debited or credited by the matched premium, so no separate RTGS transaction is needed.
There are no transaction charges for the e-Kuber PSLC module; tax treatment is for banks to determine 'in accordance with the applicable tax laws'.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RB-IOS, 2026, callers to RBI's Contact Centre (toll-free 14448) can speak to its personnel in English, Hindi and how many regional languages?

options.text: Eight
Ten
Twelve
Twenty-two

solution.explanation: The Contact Centre guides complainants on the grievance redress mechanism and complaint status. Its personnel are available in English, Hindi and ten regional languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Marathi, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Telugu and Tamil).
solution.why_others_wrong: Eight and twelve are wrong counts; 22 is the number of languages in the Eighth Schedule, not the Contact Centre's languages.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Ten

fact_checks.claim: The facility to connect to Contact Center personnel is available ... 'in English, Hindi and ten regional languages' (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Marathi, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Telugu, Tamil).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RB-IOS, 2026, the RBI Ombudsman or Deputy Ombudsman may help the complainant and the regulated entity reach a mutually acceptable settlement. By which means can this be done, according to RBI's FAQs?

options.text: Arbitration, mediation or adjudication
Conciliation only, in a meeting held in person
Facilitation, advisory or conciliation
Negotiation through a Lok Adalat or a civil court

solution.explanation: A maintainable complaint can end in settlement, an Award or rejection. Settlement may be reached through facilitation, advisory or conciliation; if the grievance is resolved or the complainant accepts the resolution, the complaint is closed as settled. Conciliation meetings may be attended in person or online.
steps: Settlement via facilitation, advisory or conciliation
solution.why_others_wrong: The scheme does not use arbitration or court adjudication, and conciliation is neither the only mode nor restricted to in-person meetings.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Facilitation, advisory or conciliation

fact_checks.claim: Settlement: The RBI Ombudsman or RBI Deputy Ombudsman may help the complainant and the Regulated Entity arrive at a mutually acceptable resolution. 'This may be done through facilitation, advisory or conciliation.'

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following NBFCs is NOT covered by RB-IOS, 2026, even though it is registered with RBI?

options.text: A deposit-taking NBFC-Investment and Credit Company
An NBFC-Microfinance Institution with customer interface and assets of ₹250 crore
A gold-loan NBFC with customer interface and assets of ₹1,000 crore
An NBFC-Infrastructure Finance Company with assets of ₹5,000 crore

solution.explanation: RB-IOS covers NBFCs that accept deposits or have customer interface with assets of ₹100 crore and above, but excludes Housing Finance Companies, Core Investment Companies, IDF-NBFCs, NBFC-IFCs, NOFHCs, Primary Dealers and Mortgage Guarantee Companies. An NBFC-IFC is therefore outside the scheme whatever its size.
steps: Check excluded types: HFC, CIC, IDF-NBFC, NBFC-IFC, NOFHC, PD, MGC
solution.why_others_wrong: A deposit-taking NBFC and customer-facing NBFCs with assets of ₹100 crore or more are covered.
solution.final_answer: Option D: An NBFC-Infrastructure Finance Company with assets of ₹5,000 crore

fact_checks.claim: NBFCs: all NBFCs registered with RBI, excluding Housing Finance Companies, Core Investment Companies, IDF-NBFCs, NBFC-IFCs, NOFHCs, Primary Dealers and Mortgage Guarantee Companies, which either are authorized to accept deposits or have customer interface with asset size of Rs 100 crore and above.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In 2026 Kiran first complains to her bank about a disputed debit from 2019, after the period of limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963 has expired. The bank rejects it and she approaches the RBI Ombudsman within 90 days. Under RB-IOS, 2026, her complaint is:

options.text: Maintainable, because she approached the Ombudsman within 90 days of the bank's reply
Not maintainable, because her complaint to the bank was made after the limitation period expired
Maintainable, because there is no limit on the amount or age of a dispute under the scheme
Not maintainable, because complaints about debits must go to the card network first

solution.explanation: Besides the 30-day and 90-day timelines, the complaint to the regulated entity must itself have been made before the expiry of the limitation period under the Limitation Act, 1963. Complaints where the complaint to the RE was made after that period are not maintainable.
steps: Check limitation for the original complaint to the RE → expired
solution.why_others_wrong: Meeting the 90-day window does not cure the limitation defect; 'no limit' applies only to the amount in dispute; there is no rule routing debit complaints to the card network.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Not maintainable, because her complaint to the bank was made after the limitation period expired

fact_checks.claim: Non-maintainable: 'Complaints where the complaint to the Regulated Entity was made after expiry of the limitation period under the Limitation Act, 1963.'

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Two customers with apparently similar grievances receive different outcomes from the RBI Ombudsman. According to RBI's FAQs on RB-IOS, 2026, which statement best explains this?

options.text: Similar-looking cases may differ in facts, documents, relief sought and applicable instructions, and the Ombudsman considers principles of banking law and practice and RBI directions
The Ombudsman is bound by the earlier decision in a similar case, so the second outcome must be an error
Each RBI Ombudsman office follows its own local rules, so outcomes vary by State
Outcomes depend only on whether the regulated entity agrees to settle

solution.explanation: The FAQs say cases that appear similar may differ in facts, documents, relief sought, applicable regulatory instructions and conduct of the parties. The Scheme lets the Ombudsman consider the principles of banking law and practice, RBI directions/instructions and other relevant factors.
steps: Look at facts, documents, relief and conduct
Apply banking law and practice and RBI instructions
solution.why_others_wrong: There is no binding precedent rule; handling is jurisdiction-neutral ('One Nation One Ombudsman'), not State-wise; and Awards can be passed without the entity's agreement.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Similar-looking cases may differ in facts, documents, relief sought and applicable instructions, and the Ombudsman considers principles of banking law and practice and RBI directions

fact_checks.claim: 'Cases that appear similar may differ in facts, documents, relief sought,' applicable regulatory instructions and conduct of the parties. The Scheme enables the RBI Ombudsman to consider the principles of banking law and practice, RBI directions/instructions/guidelines/regulations and other relevant factors while deciding a complaint.

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Under RB-IOS, 2026, on which of the following grounds may an RBI Deputy Ombudsman (as distinct from the RBI Ombudsman) reject a complaint?
I. The complaint is non-maintainable under Clause 10 of the Scheme.
II. The complaint requires elaborate documentary and oral evidence, making the proceedings inappropriate.
III. A case on the same cause of action is filed before a court or tribunal while the complaint is being examined.
Select the correct answer:

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III

solution.explanation: The Deputy Ombudsman can reject a complaint only on the grounds in Clause 16(1): non-maintainability under Clause 10, no deficiency in service (suggestions, queries and the like), or a case on the same cause of action being filed before a court or other forum during examination. Rejection because elaborate evidence is needed is among the RBI Ombudsman's wider Clause 16 grounds.
steps: I and III are Clause 16(1) grounds
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing II are wrong because that ground is exercised by the RBI Ombudsman, not the Deputy Ombudsman.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: The RBI Deputy Ombudsman may reject a complaint at any stage on any of the grounds specified in Clause 16(1): the complaint is non-maintainable under Clause 10; it does not disclose any deficiency in service; or a case on the same cause of action is filed before a Court, Tribunal, Arbitrator or other forum.
The RBI Ombudsman may reject a complaint at any stage if, among other grounds, it requires consideration of elaborate documentary and oral evidence (Clause 16).

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: On 22 September 2026, RBI finalised instructions, based on feedback on draft directions of July 2025, on the novation of which contracts?

options.text: Housing loan agreements
Bank guarantees in trade finance
Gold loan contracts of NBFCs
OTC derivative contracts

RBI's circular of 22 September 2026 finalised the instructions on novation of OTC derivative contracts, issued in draft on 9 July 2025, and inserted them into four existing directions (OTC forex, rupee interest rate derivatives, G-sec forwards and credit derivatives). They apply to novations on or after the circular's date.
steps: Final: 22 September 2026, for OTC derivative contracts
solution.why_others_wrong: The circular is about OTC derivatives, not loans, guarantees or gold loans.
solution.final_answer: Option D: OTC derivative contracts

fact_checks.claim: Refers to the 'draft Reserve Bank of India (Novation of OTC Derivative Contracts) Directions, 2025' issued on July 09, 2025; 'Based on the feedback received, the instructions related to the OTC derivative contracts have been finalised.'

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: By a circular effective 1 October 2026, RBI allowed a bank's Board to delegate the monitoring of progress in implementing cassette swaps in ATMs to:

options.text: A Committee of Executives
The RBI Regional Office
The bank's statutory central auditor
The National Payments Corporation of India

solution.explanation: Under RBI's 2022 circular, banks were to replace ATM cash cassettes with pre-loaded ones (cassette swaps). The 1 October 2026 amendment, issued alongside the 2026 governance amendment directions, lets the Board delegate monitoring of implementation to a Committee of Executives.
steps: 2026 change: monitoring may be delegated to a Committee of Executives
solution.why_others_wrong: Monitoring is an internal governance task; it is not handed to RBI, auditors or NPCI.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A Committee of Executives

fact_checks.claim: 'monitoring the progress of implementation of cassette swap may be delegated by the Board to a Committee of Executives' (substituted w.e.f. October 1, 2026).

questions.question_text: On 1 October 2026, after reviewing its instructions on currency management, RBI withdrew the instructions that had been consolidated into function-wise Master Directions or had become obsolete. How many were listed for withdrawal?

solution.explanation: RBI reviewed its currency management instructions, consolidated the extant ones into function-wise Master Directions (for example on exchange of notes and coins, and counterfeit notes) and withdrew the 268 instructions listed in the Annex, including obsolete or redundant ones dating from 1976 onward.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other figures do not match the number of instructions listed in the Annex.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 268

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's KYC amendment directions of 18 September 2026 (for small finance banks and regional rural banks, among others) extended the option of submitting an 'original certified copy' of documents, earlier available to NRIs and PIOs, to which customers?

options.text: Resident senior citizens
Self-help groups
Foreign diplomats in India
Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)

solution.explanation: The amendments let the bank obtain an original certified copy of KYC documents from FPIs too, as already allowed for NRIs and PIOs. The copy may be certified by, among others, overseas branches of Indian scheduled commercial banks, partner overseas banks, a Notary Public abroad, a Court Magistrate, a Judge or the Indian Embassy/Consulate.
solution.why_others_wrong: The change concerns non-resident customers who cannot easily present documents in person; the other groups were not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)

fact_checks.claim: Amended para 5(1)(v): for NRIs, PIOs 'and Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), the bank may alternatively obtain the original certified copy, certified by any one of the following'.
